extracted.intended_audience: department legal and financial officers, government attorneys, comptroller and procurement officials (Secretaries of War/Defense-level staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and principles for what federal appropriations may lawfully be spent on, how to construe specific vs. general appropriations, and which incidental or related expenses may be charged to particular appropriations (with examples from Army/War Department practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expenditure limited to appropriation; donations do not bypass appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary (or department) could not let a contract or employ labor, or purchase materials, in excess of the appropriation; if a sum is furnished or turned over as proposed, the sum could not be expended on the work until it had been appropriated for the work by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donations or offered funds cannot be used to exceed statutory appropriations. Suggested arrangements (e.g., third party purchases and transfer of materials/labor) may be used to accomplish work without directly expending beyond the appropriation (example discussed re: Daughters of the American Revolution donation). (G.1662, Aug. 23, 1895; O.12340, Apr. 2, 1902.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposited state or third-party funds treated as quasi public money subject to appropriation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Money deposited with the Secretary (e.g., sums transferred by a State and deposited in the subtreasury) should be considered quasi public money of the United States and should remain on deposit until disbursed in conformity to the act of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funds earmarked or deposited for a purpose are still subject to federal appropriation law and must be disbursed only in conformity with the authorizing statute. (G.13999, Feb. 24, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary surveys/plans may be chargeable to project appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Expenses incident to preliminary surveys, plans, etc., in connection with completion of a plan for enlargement or erection of buildings may be chargeable to the appropriation for the erection of the buildings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work or services that are preliminary but necessary to effectuate the authorized project can be paid from the project's appropriation (examples: surveys and data-gathering preliminary to acquisition or improvement). (G.15553, Apr. 29, 1902; C.16479, June 18, 1904.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific appropriation limits legal expenditure to intended object and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: When a special appropriation is made for a certain object, it expresses the amount of public money which can legally be expended for that object and ordinarily cannot be expended for the partial accomplishment only of that object if that would defeat the congressional purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Congress appropriates for 'construction complete of a sewerage system' the expectation is completion within the appropriation; expenditures that would only partially accomplish the object (leaving the project incomplete) are generally unlawful unless circumstances show the partial work accomplishes the congressional purpose. (Cases: 55 F. 364; C.3453; C.55441.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Designated-multiple-items apportionment rule
rubrics_metrics.description: If an appropriation is made for multiple specified places or items, the entire sum cannot lawfully be expended on one of the designated places/items alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An appropriation for construction of three ice piers 'at certain designated places' may not be spent wholly on constructing one pier. Funds should be applied in accordance with the designation unless Congress indicates otherwise. (C.10854, July 18, 1901.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific appropriations are exclusive of general appropriations (priority rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an appropriation is made for a specific object it is the only one applicable to that object, although a more general appropriation might otherwise have applied; the general cannot be used to supplement the specific unless Congress authorizes it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of whether an appropriation is 'specific' or 'general' is outcome-determinative; where doubtful, the head of the department may exercise discretion. If two appropriations are both applicable and neither is exclusive, they may be cumulative and used at the department head's discretion. (See multiple Comptroller decisions cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictive construction of general words following specific enumeration (ejusdem generis application)
rubrics_metrics.description: General words following the enumeration of special articles or classes are to receive a restrictive construction limited to articles or classes of like kind with those specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases like 'and for all other absolutely necessary expenses' are read as limited to items similar to those enumerated in the appropriation (example: covers equipment peculiar to the needs of the school but not wholly unrelated items). (C.18490, Sept. 7, 1905; C.13100, Sept. 22, 1903.)

rubrics_metrics.name: The phrase 'all other absolutely necessary expenses' covers similar necessary items but remains limited by context
rubrics_metrics.description: Language in an appropriation such as 'and for all other absolutely necessary expenses' will include items similar to those enumerated and other necessary incidental expenses reasonably related to the purpose, but may not extend to items more properly part of a different appropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: such language covered special equestrian equipment or telegrams for a court of inquiry, and included paying a reward for discovering vandalism; but it was doubtful (or disallowed) to include electric fixtures intended to become part of a building or the purchase of a post-exchange laundry building. (C.20719; C.20754; C.15026.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation for purchase/distribution of relief supplies does not authorize reimbursement of private parties
rubrics_metrics.description: An act authorizing the purchase and distribution of subsistence stores, supplies, and materials for relief does not authorize the use of the appropriation to reimburse private parties for relief they have furnished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriations permitting purchase/distribution by the government do not imply authority to pay private donors for past relief absent express authorization. (C.6078; C.734; C.7483; C.11077.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Project appropriations generally not available to pay damages or unrelated personal claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Money appropriated for improvement projects (e.g., rivers and harbors) is not available for payment of damages suffered by individuals due to negligence of government employees or defective construction, nor for payment for personal services or certain employee allowances unless statute authorizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: funds for river and harbor improvement cannot be used to pay civilian physicians treating employees, pay damages for loss of personal effects, or pay services rendered in extinguishing a fire on a government dredge. Statutory authority is required to divert project funds to such claims. (Various Comptroller decisions cited; 54 F. 390; C.1696; C.23069.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidental costs of acquiring land are chargeable to land purchase appropriation; condemnation costs usually from DOJ
rubrics_metrics.description: Expenses of procuring abstracts, certificates, evidence of title, recording deeds, making surveys, and paying taxes necessary to purchase land are properly chargeable to the appropriation for purchase of the land; expenses connected with condemnation proceedings are ordinarily payable from appropriations for the Department of Justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where land is purchased with an appropriation, normal acquisition expenses (abstracts, surveys, recording, necessary tax searches) may be paid from that appropriation. If title defects necessitate condemnation, costs of condemnation proceedings generally arise from Justice Department funds. (C.2546; C.15698; C.29072; C.15110.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing relief appropriations: replacement, travel/subsistence, and non-transferability
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuing appropriations for disaster relief authorize the Secretary to use means at hand or procure supplies and to issue them to beneficiaries; they permit purchases to replace issued stores without regard to fiscal year, reimburse ordinary travel expenses (mileage) for relief officers, and charge travel/subsistence incurred while administering relief to the appropriation; unexpended balances cannot be applied to different later disasters in different localities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: public resolutions authorizing relief permitted replacing stores issued to beneficiaries and charging travel/subsistence incidental to relief work to the appropriation, but a balance from one disaster could not be used for relief of sufferers from an unrelated later flood. (C.23289; decisions on May 22, 1908; Sept. 27, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic and temporal limits of relief appropriations
rubrics_metrics.description: An appropriation for relief tied to a specified area or occasion does not authorize relief outside the designated geographical scope or long after the statutory purpose (e.g., an appropriation to relieve the French West Indies does not authorize relief to the Danish West Indies or grants years later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriations are constrained by the geographic and timing language of the statute; requests for aid outside those limits or long after the event may be refused. (C.13008; C.16188.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation for construction does not authorize purchase of existing buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: An appropriation 'for the construction, operation, and maintenance' of laundries in Army posts does not make funds available for purchasing a post-exchange laundry building with its machinery and fixtures already constructed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriations that authorize construction are not to be read as authority to buy pre-existing structures unless the appropriation language or subsequent statute expressly permits purchase. (C.15026, Jan. 22, 1912.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Government may expend on improvements on lands without title when benefit assured; easements often sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no legal objection to spending public money on improvements on lands to which title has not been acquired (unless a statute forbids it), provided the Government will be assured of receiving the benefit; an easement is generally sufficient for constructing levees, pipelines, or using highways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: appropriations for transportation or 'roads, walks, wharves, and drainage' can be expended on public highways or sidewalks where title or easement is not in the U.S.; monuments may be erected without acquiring title to the site. (C.15264; C.22355; C.23041; C.7842.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Repairs to public highways on federal reservations chargeable if military benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a public highway runs through a military reservation and repairs would be useful for military purposes, the expense of repairing such a road may be a legal charge against funds for the general appropriation for army transportation or related accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although highway repair is generally a local government duty, if the repair serves military purposes it may be funded from federal transportation appropriations (examples: repairs on highways through military reservations or national cemeteries). (C.3683, Nov. 27, 1897; C.20373, Apr. 28, 1910.)
